title: The Last Leaf
author: O. Henry
themes: hope and the will to live

lessonPlan.title: The Last Leaf unit
lessonPlan.author: O. Henry
lessonPlan.editionNote: Reading text: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Trimmed_Lamp_(1907)/The_Last_Leaf (revision 13324710), cleaned for Liber et Libri.
lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 6–10 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Last Leaf.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Last Leaf: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

lessonPlan.middleSchoolTrack: Short story: read whole in one 90-minute lesson (assign longer stories as pre-reading). Middle School prompts use the full text when the grade tags include 6–8; otherwise teacher-selected passages.
lessonPlan.schedule: One 90-minute lesson (the whole story), with an optional take-home essay
essentialQuestions: What does The Last Leaf suggest about hope and the will to live?
What does The Last Leaf suggest about art and sacrifice?
What does The Last Leaf suggest about friendship?
objectives: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly and implicitly.
Determine themes and analyze their development over the course of the story.
Analyze how characters, setting and point of view interact.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in the text.
Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.

wholeBookTest.title: The Last Leaf: whole-book test

items.prompt: What does Johnsy believe will happen when the last leaf falls?

options: An old painter who has never painted his masterpiece

items.prompt: Why does the last leaf never fall?
options: Behrman painted it on the wall

items.prompt: In the line “Then she swaggered into Johnsy’s room with her drawing board, whistling ragtime.”, what does “swaggered” most nearly mean?
options: walked or behaved in a boastful, arrogant way

items.prompt: In the line “A mite of a little woman with blood thinned by California zephyrs was hardly fair game for the red-fisted, short-breathed old duffer.”, what does “zephyrs” most nearly mean?
options: walked or behaved in a boastful, arrogant way

items.prompt: As used in the story (“Then she swaggered into Johnsy’s room with her drawing board, whistling ragtime.”), what does “swaggered” mean?
options: walked or behaved in a boastful, arrogant way
one who destroys or lays waste

items.prompt: As used in the story (“A mite of a little woman with blood thinned by California zephyrs was hardly fair game for the red-fisted, short-breathed old duffer.”), what does “zephyrs” mean?
As used in the story (“Still dark green near its stem, but with its serrated edges tinted with the yellow of dissolution and decay, it hung bravely from a branch s”), what does “serrated” mean?
options: relating to the medical treatment of patients
relating to the gallant, protective code of knights

items.prompt: As used in the story (“When it was light enough Johnsy, the merciless, commanded that the shade be raised.”), what does “merciless” mean?
options: one who destroys or lays waste
walked or behaved in a boastful, arrogant way

items.prompt: As used in the story (“They had met at the table d’hote of an Eighth street “Delmonico’s,” and found their tastes in art, chicory salad and bishop sleeves so conge”), what does “congenial” mean?

answerKey.answer: An old painter who has never painted his masterpiece
Behrman painted it on the wall
walked or behaved in a boastful, arrogant way
walked or behaved in a boastful, arrogant way

shortAnswer: Explain how hope and the will to live develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how art and sacrifice develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how friendship develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the story's central concerns (hope and the will to live, art and sacrifice, friendship) and argue how the ending reframes it.

essayAssignments.title: Essay: Hope and the will to live
essayAssignments.theme: hope and the will to live

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what The Last Leaf teaches about hope and the will to live. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how O. Henry develops hope and the will to live in The Last Leaf. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how O. Henry develops hope and the will to live across The Last Leaf. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of The Last Leaf (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of hope and the will to live. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of hope and the will to live in The Last Leaf. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how O. Henry's choices in The Last Leaf (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of hope and the will to live, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places The Last Leaf's treatment of hope and the will to live in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on hope and the will to live in The Last Leaf that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on hope and the will to live in The Last Leaf. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about hope and the will to live in The Last Leaf, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on hope and the will to live in The Last Leaf, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
